why: Count the density: 5 nav rows, 7 pull requests with amber or green counts and one spinner, and 12 drift rows each carrying name, property, value and status, with hierarchy built from 13px type and one selected row; the order summary is rendered twice with three CSS overrides on the second copy, so the slider reveals the exact drifts the list names, and the audience switch swaps every value for a file and line.

Each visual half is a working fragment with its own data (7 token rows with Figma, Build and Uses columns, 6 named snapshots against 3 decided values, a 2-comment thread with a status chip and 2 actions), colour lands only on the values that drifted, and the tile widths change row to row so no two rows share a rhythm.

The logo strip became 12 instances of the product's own check row, each with 6 data points (identicon, team, pull request number, title, drift status, run time) and titles naming that customer's actual work, so the proof reads as live activity and the only colour is amber or green status.

Notice the 3 dot states (past, current, future), the line that fills by i/3, the single tab stop with wrapping arrow keys, and that the 8 panels show a different artefact for each step (config, terminal, component, JSON, request, response) with the same ids throughout, where a generic page would show 4 numbered cards.

Notice how much the table carries with no cards at all: 13 rows across 3 sticky groups, real limits mixed with ticks and dashes, a first column that explains billing, and a measured --plans offset that docks group heads under the plan row; the recommended plan gets only an accent outline, and on phones one data-plan attribute reduces it to a single column.
